newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt foreign reserves surpass $20 bln in May.
newsitem.headline: Egypt foreign reserves surpass $20 bln in May.

text.p: Egypt's foreign reserves have surpassed $20 billion, enough to cover imports for more than a year, but the country still needs to attract foreign investment to achieve growth targets, economists said on Tuesday.
The $20 billion is Egypt's highest foreign reserves ever, said government economist Hani Dimian. It is equivalent to the country's total external debt service requirements for 13 years.
"The external situation for Egypt is healthy," said Arvind Subramanian, International Monetary Fund representative. "Reserves are fairly high relative to imports and...debt."
The Central Bank's August bulletin said foreign reserves were $20.199 billion in May up from $19.746 billion in April.
Given 1996/97 import figures of $14.9 billion, Egypt's foreign reserves mean that it can pay for 16 to 17 months of imports without using exports to finance them, said Dimian.
Average debt service of $1.5 billion a year "allows Egypt to finance its total debt service for some 13 years," he said.

But Egypt's priorities are "attracting investments," said Dimian. "In Egypt there are not enough funds to finance investment needed to achieve growth targets and make them more feasible. We must invite foreign investment."
He said the import has improved from consumer goods to investment, intermediate and raw materials.
Growth is forecast at 5.5 percent to 5.7 for 1997/98.

"It's not the most useful way to build growth, by having more and more reserves," said an international economist in Cairo. "My understanding is it's one of the largest official reserves of all the developing countries."
But he said there was a feeling that "Egypt could go faster on economic reforms and could liberalise more quickly."
Egypt has embarked in earnest on an economic reform programme since last year which highlights privatisation, attracting private investment and liberalising trade.

The country is also reforming its financial sector. The European Commission is focusing on four core programmes in Egypt, including bank supervision and foreign asset management. One official said a public tender for a foreign asset management adviser is expected to be issued in August or after the month.

"Last year they used to buy treasury bills from the United States. I think now they are trying to do it better, at least look at the interest rates...also in Asia and Europe. Their asset management has to be revised," the economist said.
A central bank official said: "We are still investing in treasury bills in the United States."

The Central Bank said foreign reserves have risen by $1.655 billion since May, 1996. "Reserves have increased on the strength of capital inflows," said Subramanian. He said the inflows were a positive sign because they meant more resources for investment and show endorsement by international markets.
Dimian said capital inflows were $1.5 billion in 1996/97, with $900 million in portfolio and $650 million in direct.

Subramanian said Egypt's reform-minded planners would have to be vigilant to ward off any inflationary pressures in the long term. "A surge (in capital inflows) creates challenges on macro-economic management which bear watching. They could create inflationary pressures down the road. It warrants vigilance."
However, the fall in interest rates is bringing domestic rates in line with international rates, Dimian said.
Year-on-year inflation fell to 4.8 percent in June, its lowest level in more than six years, from 4.9 percent in May and 8.3 percent in June 1996, according to government statistics.
"What is happening now is price stability, which means price changes are moderate and can be anticipated by the market. It is a more advanced stage than just falling inflation," Dimian said.
